stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Immunologist Lena Okafor and colleagues found that adults who received a tuberculosis vaccine mounted stronger innate immune responses to several unrelated viruses three months later. Okafor concludes that the vaccine "trains" innate immune cells, giving recipients broad protection that reaches well beyond tuberculosis.

Text 2
Okafor's findings certainly offer encouraging evidence that innate immune cells can be trained. Still, when the same volunteers were retested, the heightened response had faded in most of them within a year. It's important to consider, then, that whatever broad protection the vaccine confers may be temporary.
choices: A tuberculosis vaccine can strengthen innate immune responses to pathogens other than tuberculosis.
The broad protection offered by a tuberculosis vaccine is likely to fade within a year.
Okafor's results offer little real evidence that innate immune cells can be trained.
The vaccine's effect on innate immune cells lasts long enough to protect recipients permanently.
explanation: Text 2 opens with a concession: Okafor's findings "certainly offer encouraging evidence" that innate cells can be trained. Then it turns on "Still" and adds a limit, which is that the effect may not last. Since Text 2 accepts the main finding, both authors agree that the vaccine strengthens innate responses to other pathogens. They differ only on how long that lasts.

B.why: You picked the caveat that only Text 2 raises. Okafor never says the protection fades, so you can't assume she would agree. A shared statement has to be something both authors accept.

C.why: You read "Still" as a full rejection. Text 2 says explicitly that the findings "certainly offer encouraging evidence." It limits Okafor's conclusion without dismissing it.

D.why: Okafor claims broad protection, not permanent protection, so this is a stronger version of her view than she gives. Text 2 also suggests the effect may be temporary, so neither author supports this.

Text 2

The rise in downtown cycling was probably caused by something other than the lanes.
Protected bike lanes contributed to the increase in cycling in downtown Halverton.
Protected bike lanes raise cycling by roughly the same amount in every part of a city.

A.why: This is the limit that only Text 2 adds. Duarte says nothing about outlying neighborhoods, and his call for other cities to copy Halverton suggests he would not accept it.

B.why: You treated the "But" as full disagreement. Text 2 explicitly says the downtown lanes "clearly mattered," so its author does not credit the rise to some other cause.

D.why: Duarte never claims equal effects everywhere, so this is a stronger version of his view than he gives. Text 2's outlying-neighborhood data also show the effect was not equal.

The coating can recover much of its strength after a single crack forms.

Both authors accept that the coating restores much of its strength after one crack, which is choice B.

A.why: Text 2 rules this out directly: capsules release resin 'only once', so a region that keeps cracking soon runs out. Text 1 never claims repeated healing at the same spot either. It reports recovery after a crack, not after many cracks.

D.why: This is Text 1's conclusion, the claim Text 2 was written to limit. You saw that Text 2 begins by agreeing and missed the caveat after 'Yet': because the capsules run out, the protection may not last long, so Author 2 would not accept 'greatly extend'.
